items.q: Why is `with open("tasks.txt") as f:` preferred over plain `f = open("tasks.txt")`?
options: The `with` block closes the file automatically when done, even if an error happens
It is the only way to read a file
It makes the file load faster

explain.right: A with block guarantees the file is closed when the block ends (or errors), so you never leak an open file handle.
explain.wrong: It doesn't change speed or encrypt anything, and files can be opened without `with` (you'd just have to close them yourself).

items.q: A file `log.txt` has data in it. You run `open("log.txt", "w")`. What happens to the existing contents?
options: They're erased — mode "w" empties the file before writing; use "a" to append instead
Nothing can happen until you write
They're kept and new writes go after them

explain.right: Opening in "w" truncates the file immediately, so the old contents are gone; "a" (append) adds without erasing.
explain.wrong: "w" does not keep or back up old contents; the erase happens on open, before any write.

items.q: Why is `except FileNotFoundError:` better than a bare `except:` when loading a file that might not exist?
options: Bare except is required by Python
A bare except catches every error — including typos and Ctrl-C — and hides real bugs; naming the exception handles only the case you expect

explain.right: Catching the specific exception handles the expected problem and lets unexpected errors surface instead of being silently swallowed.
explain.wrong: They don't behave the same; a bare except is a known anti-pattern because it masks bugs, and it is never required.

items.q: When reading a traceback to find why your program crashed, where is the most directly relevant line usually found?
options: Tracebacks never point to a line
At the bottom — the last lines show the exception type/message and the deepest call where it failed

explain.right: An exception is a signal: the bottom of the traceback names the error type, its message, and the innermost line that triggered it.
explain.wrong: The top shows the outer call chain; the actionable detail (type + failing line) is at the bottom.

items.q: In one or two sentences, explain why raising a clear exception can be better than silently ignoring a bad input.
rubric: An exception is an explicit signal that something is wrong, with a type and message
Silently ignoring hides the problem and can cause worse, harder-to-find bugs later
The caller can catch and handle a raised exception or see it clearly during development

explain.right: Good answers frame exceptions as honest signals that surface problems early, versus silent failures that hide them.
explain.wrong: A weak answer says 'exceptions are bad / always catch them' — the point is that a loud, specific failure beats a hidden one.
